In what year was Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor born?
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor: Andrew was born second in the line of succession to the British throne and is eighth as of 2026.
In what year was Boris Yeltsin born?
Boris Yeltsin: Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin (1 February 1931 – 23 April 2007) was a Soviet and Russian politician who served as President of Russia from 1991 to 1999.
In what year was Henry VII of England born?
Henry VII of England: Henry was the son of Edmund Tudor, 1st Earl of Richmond, and Lady Margaret Beaufort.
In what year did Kim Jong Il die?
Kim Jong Il: Posthumously, Kim Jong Il was declared an Eternal Leader of the Workers' Party of Korea (WPK).
In what year did Charlemagne die?
Charlemagne's reign was marked by political and social changes that had lasting influence on Europe throughout the Middle Ages.
In what year did Louis XVI die?
Louis XVI: The son of Louis, Dauphin of France (son and heir apparent of King Louis XV), and Maria Josepha of Saxony, Louis became the new Dauphin when his father died in 1765.
In what year was Habsburg monarchy founded?
Habsburg monarchy: It became extinct in the male line in 1740, but continued through the female line as the House of Habsburg-Lorraine.
In what year was Republican Party (United States) founded?
Republican Party (United States): The Republican Party, also known as the Grand Old Party (GOP), is a right-wing to far-right political party in the United States.
In what year was Big Bang discovered?
Big Bang: The Big Bang is a physical theory that describes how the universe expanded from an initial state of high density and temperature.

Heaven's Gate (religious group): Marshall Applewhite. Heaven's Gate was an American new religious movement known primarily for the mass suicide of its members in 1997.

In which country did the Battle of the Camel take place?
Battle of the Camel: Iraq. The Battle of the Camel, also known as the Battle of Basra (Arabic: معركة الجمل, romanized: Maʿrakat al-Jamal) took place in 656 CE outside of Basra in Iraq.
In which country is Republican Proposal based?
Republican Proposal: Argentina. Republican Proposal (Spanish: Propuesta Republicana), usually referred to by its abbreviation PRO, is a political party in Argentina.
In which country was the Caliphate of Córdoba?
Caliphate of Córdoba: Spain. The Emirate of Córdoba, and from 929, the Caliphate of Córdoba, was an Arab Islamic state ruled by the Umayyad dynasty from 756 to 1031.
In which country was the Sultanate of Ternate?
Sultanate of Ternate: Indonesia. The Ternate kingdom was established by Momole Cico, the first leader of Ternate, with the title Baab Mashur Malamo, traditionally in 1257.
In which country is Battle of Shanghai?
Battle of Shanghai: Taiwan. It resulted in the Japanese capture of Shanghai and heavy destruction to the city.
In which country is People's Action Party based?
People's Action Party: Singapore. The PAP was established in 1954 as a conventional centre-left party.
In which country did the Kataeb Party take place?
Kataeb Party: Lebanon. The Phalangists were responsible for the Black Saturday massacre, the Tel al-Zaatar massacre, Ehden massacre, and the Karantina massacre.
In which country is Chakri dynasty?
Chakri dynasty: Thailand. The Chakri dynasty, unofficially the House of Chakri, is the current reigning dynasty of the Kingdom of Thailand.
In which country was Great Smog of London?
Great Smog of London: United Kingdom. The Great Smog was a severe air pollution event that affected London, England, in December 1952.
Which of these was an official language of the Kingdom of Sardinia?
Kingdom of Sardinia: Italian. Beginning in 1324, James and his successors conquered the island of Sardinia and established de facto their de jure authority.
Which of these was an official language of the Aztec Empire?
Aztec Empire: Classical Nahuatl. Its people and civil society are historiographically referred to as the Aztecs or the Culhua-Mexica.
Which of these was an official language of Congo Free State?
Congo Free State: French. It was privately owned by King Leopold II, the constitutional monarch of the Kingdom of Belgium.
Which country used the Sicilian piastra as its official currency?

The Sicilian piastra is the official currency of Kingdom of Sicily. It was a successor state of the County of Sicily, which had been founded in 1071 during the Norman conquest of the southern peninsula.
This member of the Imperial House of Japan reigned as the 125th emperor from 1989 until his abdication in 2019, with his era named the Heisei era — who is he?
Akihito (born 23 December 1933) is a member of the Imperial House of Japan who reigned as the 125th emperor of Japan from 7 January 1989 until his abdication on 30 April 2019.
This political philosophy advocates for abolishing authority and hierarchy, and is described as the libertarian wing of the socialist movement. What ideology is this?
Anarchism is a political philosophy and movement that seeks to abolish all institutions that perpetuate authority, coercion, or hierarchy, primarily targeting the state and capitalism.

Convicted as a war criminal for his role in the deportation of Dutch Jews while serving as Reichskommissar of the Netherlands, this man had briefly been Austria's chancellor before the 1938 Anschluss — who was he?

Arthur Seyss-Inquart (Austrian German; 22 July 1892 - 16 October 1946) was an Austrian Nazi politician and convicted war criminal who served as Chancellor of Austria in 1938 for two days before the Anschluss.
This 1944 amphibious assault on a Pacific island put Japan's home cities within range of B-29 bombers and triggered the resignation of Prime Minister Hideki Tōjō — which engagement?
Battle of Saipan was an amphibious assault launched by the United States against the Empire of Japan during the Pacific campaign of World War II between 15 June and 9 July 1944.
Originally a townhouse built for a duke in 1703, this London landmark was bought by George III in 1761 as a home for Queen Charlotte — what is it?
Buckingham Palace is the official residence and the administrative headquarters of the monarch of the United Kingdom in London.
Writing mainly in Russian but also in his native tongue, this author became one of the most celebrated figures in all of Kyrgyz literature — who is he?
Chinghiz Aitmatov (12 December 1928 - 10 June 2008) was a Kyrgyz author who wrote mainly in Russian, but also in Kyrgyz.
Taking office at just 35, this Ecuadorian businessman-turned-politician became the second-youngest president in his country's history. Who is he?
Daniel Noboa (born 30 November 1987) is an Ecuadorian politician and businessman serving as the 48th and current president of Ecuador since 2023.
First held on April 22, 1970, this globally coordinated annual event rallies support for environmental protection — what is it?

Earth Day is an annual event on April 22 to demonstrate support for environmental protection. This day of nature's equipoise was later sanctioned in a proclamation written by McConnell and signed by Secretary General U Thant at the United Nations.
This political position argues the EU is too bureaucratic, insufficiently democratic, and erodes national sovereignty, with its mildest form seeking reform rather than exit — what is it called?
Euroscepticism is a political position involving criticism of the European Union (EU) and European integration.
Rising from a career as a shipowner to minister for marine and colonies, this man served as President of France from 1895 until his death in 1899 — who is he?
Félix Faure (30 January 1841 - 16 February 1899) was President of France from 1895 until his death in 1899.
Triggered by the 1929 Wall Street crash, this decade-long global economic downturn brought mass unemployment to the US, UK, and Germany — name the era?
Great Depression was a severe global economic downturn from 1929 to 1939.

Raised on a farm outside Hamilton before lecturing in politics at the University of Auckland, this Labour figure went on to lead her country for nearly a decade and later ran the UN's development programme — who is she?

Helen Clark (born 26 February 1950) is a New Zealand politician who served as the 37th prime minister of New Zealand from 1999 to 2008 and was the administrator of the United Nations Development Programme from 2009 to 2017.

Leading a party called the Free Voters since 2018, this German politician serves as Bavaria's deputy minister president and its state minister for economic affairs, regional development, and energy — who is he?

Hubert Aiwanger (born 26 January 1971) is a German politician and party leader of the Free Voters since 2018, the Deputy Minister President of Bavaria and Bavarian Minister of Economic affairs, Regional Development and Energy.
A scion of a family that owns the Hyatt hotel chain, this Democratic politician has served as the 43rd governor of Illinois since 2019 — who is he?
JB Pritzker (born January 19, 1965) is an American politician, philanthropist, and businessman serving since 2019 as the 43rd governor of Illinois.

Educated at Wheaton College in the United States, this monarch became the world's youngest reigning king at age 26 when his father abdicated the throne of a small Himalayan kingdom in 2006 — who is he?
Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck (born 21 February 1980) is the current King of Bhutan, reigning since 9 December 2006.

This South African politician founded and leads a communist, black nationalist party, having previously served as president of the African National Congress's Youth League before his expulsion from the party in 2012 — who is he?
Julius Malema (born 3 March 1981) is a South African politician.

Beginning in 1881 with the crowning of a Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen prince as King Carol I and ending with King Michael I's 1947 abdication, this constitutional monarchy grew from an earlier union of Moldavia and Wallachia — which kingdom?
Kingdom of Romania was a constitutional monarchy that existed from 1881 to 1947.
Championing free speech, free assembly, market economies and the rule of law, this political philosophy centers on the rights of the individual — what is it?
Liberalism is a political and moral philosophy based on the rights of the individual, liberty, consent of the governed, political equality, right to private property, and equality before the law.
A leading Indian LGBT activist who runs the Lakshya Trust, he is the probable heir to a former Maharaja and the world's first openly gay prince — who is it?
Manvendra Singh Gohil (born 23 September 1965) is a son and probable heir of former Maharaja of Rajpipla.

Before founding Herut and Likud and becoming an Israeli prime minister, he led the militant Irgun and proclaimed a 1944 revolt against British rule, behind attacks like the King David Hotel bombing — who was he?
Menachem Begin (16 August 1913 - 9 March 1992) was an Israeli politician who founded Herut and Likud and served as prime minister of Israel from 1977 to 1983.
Serving as leader of the house in Madhya Pradesh's legislative assembly, this BJP politician became the state's Chief Minister — who is he?
Mohan Yadav (born 25 March 1965) is an Indian politician serving as the current Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh and also serving as leader of the house in legislative assembly.
Founded in Turkey in 2018 by the son of a former prime minister, this Islamist movement sees itself as heir to his father's 1990s movement and the Millî Görüş ideology — which one?
New Welfare Party is an Islamist and ultraconservative political party in Turkey, founded on 23 November 2018.
Sparked by allegations of massive fraud in a 2004 presidential runoff, this wave of protests centered on Kyiv brought political upheaval to Ukraine that winter — what event is it known as?
Orange Revolution was a series of protests that led to political upheaval in Ukraine from late November 2004 to January 2005.

This ancient people settled along the southern coast of Canaan during the Iron Age, organizing their territory into a confederation of city-states with a language whose origins scholars still debate — who were they?
Philistines (LXX Koine) were an ancient people who lived along the southern coast of Canaan during the Iron Age.
Worshipped as the seventh avatar of Vishnu and considered the ideal man, this Hindu deity is the hero of an ancient epic poem — who is he?
Rama is a major deity in Hinduism.
A leading theorist of Germany's SPD, she broke away to co-found the Spartacus League that became the KPD, and wrote influentially on imperialism and revolution — who is she?
Rosa Luxemburg (5 March 1871 - 15 January 1919) was a Polish and naturalised-German Marxist theorist and revolutionary.
In Egyptian mythology, this warrior goddess also presided over medicine, carried the epithet 'the eye of Ra' as a solar deity, and was closely linked with the goddesses Hathor and Bastet. Who is she?
Sekhmet (or Sachmis, from Ancient) is a warrior goddess as well as goddess of medicine.
Serving as the 39th US vice president before resigning in 1973 under Richard Nixon, this politician was only the second VP in history to resign — the first was John C. Calhoun in 1832 — who was he?
Spiro Agnew (November 9, 1918 - September 17, 1996) was the 39th vice president of the United States, serving from 1969 until his resignation in 1973 under President Richard Nixon.
This divine hero of Greek mythology, raised by his mother Aethra and said to be the son of either the king of Athens or the sea god Poseidon, is famed for slaying the Minotaur — who is he?
Theseus (Ancient) was a divine hero in Greek mythology, famous for slaying the Minotaur.
This Roman goddess of love and beauty was said to be the ancestor of the Roman people through her son Aeneas, who fled the fall of Troy. Who is she?
Venus (mythology) (Classical) is a Roman goddess whose functions encompass love, beauty, desire, sex, fertility, prosperity, and victory.
A fierce opponent of slavery's spread, this Secretary of State served the Union through the Civil War and negotiated the treaty to buy Alaska. Who was he?

William H. Seward (May 16, 1801 - October 10, 1872) was an American politician who served as United States Secretary of State from 1861 to 1869 and earlier served as governor of New York and as a United States senator.
Elected in 2007 to the nine-member Politburo Standing Committee, the Chinese Communist Party's top decision-making body, this former senior leader once wielded major power in Beijing — who is he?
Zhou Yongkang (born December 3, 1942) is a former senior leader of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).
Born Amir, this military commander was one of ten companions promised Paradise by the Prophet Muhammad and led a large section of the Rashidun Army before dying in the Plague of Amwas — who was he?
Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah: Companion of Muhammad and military leader (583–639)

Rising to lead the Goths after the Battle of Adrianople, this first king of the Visigoths — whose Gothic name meant 'ruler of all' — served under a Roman emperor before becoming Rome's fiercest adversary in the Balkans. Who was he?
Alaric I: King of the Visigoths from 395 to 410.
Known as Operation Husky, this 1943 World War II invasion paved the way for the Allies' assault on mainland Italy, removing the nation from the war. Which major WWII campaign is this?
Allied invasion of Sicily: Part of World War 2 in 1943.

Beginning immediately after independence from Portugal in November 1975 and lasting, with interludes, until 2002, this conflict pitted the communist MPLA against the anti-communist UNITA — which nation's power struggle was this?
Angolan Civil War: 1975–2002 military conflict. The Angolan Civil War (Portuguese: Guerra Civil Angolana) was a civil war in Angola, beginning in 1975 and continuing, with interludes, until 2002.

A close aide to Egyptian presidents Nasser and Sadat, this official was allegedly a Mossad spy who fed Israel intelligence before the Yom Kippur War, then died mysteriously falling from a London balcony in 2007 — who was he?
Ashraf Marwan: Egyptian businessman and spy (1944–2007)
This Indian engineer-turned-politician served as Karnataka's 17th chief minister from 2021 to 2023 before becoming a Lok Sabha MP for Haveri — who is he?
Basavaraj Bommai: 23rd Chief Minister of Karnataka from 2021 to 2023. In July 2022, Bommai became only the second person from BJP to complete one year as chief minister of the state.

Lasting three days in September 2004, this hostage crisis in North Ossetia, Russia, took over 1,100 captives including 777 children and is considered history's deadliest attack on an educational institution — which crisis?
Beslan school siege: 2004 Russian hostage crisis and massacre.
Serving from 2017 to 2024 as France's Minister of the Economy, Finance, and Digital Sovereignty, this politician also briefly led the Ministry of the Armed Forces in October 2025 — who is he?
Prince Frederick, Duke of York and Albany
Germany's first federal minister of Circassian ancestry, this politician co-led the Greens for a decade before becoming Baden-Württemberg's minister-president in 2026 — who is he?
Cem Özdemir: German politician, Minister-President of Baden-Württemberg since 2026 (born 1965)
Commemorating the birth of Jesus and observed by billions on 25 December, its liturgical preparation season begins on the first Sunday of what?

Christmas is an annual celebration commemorating the birth of Jesus Christ, observed primarily on December 25. A liturgical feast central to Christianity, its preparation begins on the First Sunday of Advent.

Also called the War of Candia, this 24-year struggle pitted Venice and her allies — the Knights of Malta, the Papacy, France — against the Ottomans, mostly over Venice's richest overseas island. What conflict was it?
Cretan War (1645–1669): Conflict between the Republic of Venice and the Ottoman Empire (1645–1669)
This 2006 incident, believed to be the only human fatality from a stingray strike ever captured on camera, happened at Batt Reef off Australia during the filming of a nature documentary. What was it?
Death of Steve Irwin: 2006 animal encounter accident.
A retired Army colonel who led an early tank battle in the Gulf War, this author's 1997 book 'Breaking the Phalanx' argued for radical military reform — who is he?
Douglas Macgregor: U.S. Army colonel and government official (born 1947)
By leading a 2022 factional revolt that toppled Maharashtra's coalition government, this politician became the state's chief minister before later serving as deputy chief minister. Who is he?
This 13th-century marcher-lord, father of the man credited with founding the Ottoman dynasty, was granted the frontier town of Söğüt after serving the Sultanate of Rum — who was he?
Ertuğrul: Father of Osman I, died c. 1280.

Formed in 1988 as a liberal youth movement opposing Hungary's Marxist-Leninist government, this party transformed into a right-wing force that dominated Hungarian politics under Viktor Orbán — which party?
Fidesz: Political party in Hungary. It was the country's main ruling party from 1998 to 2002 and dominated Hungarian politics from 2010 to 2026 during the Orbán era.

Split by historians into 'first' and 'second' phases — the second launched by an 1830 conquest of Algiers — this overseas empire was, before World War I, the world's second-largest after Britain's — whose empire?
French colonial empire: Overseas territories controlled by France (1534–1980)
A leading orator of the Cordeliers Club, this French Revolutionary politician became Minister of Justice in 1792 and the first president of the Committee of Public Safety — who is he?
The first Democrat elected after the Civil War, he holds a singular distinction among U.S. presidents: he served two terms that didn't touch, as both the 22nd and 24th to hold the office. Who is he?
Grover Cleveland: President of the United States (1885–1889; 1893–1897)

Son of a Memphis congressman who held the same House seat for 22 years, this Tennessee Democrat represented the same district before an unsuccessful 2006 Senate bid and later became a Morgan Stanley executive — who is he?
Thomas Seymour, 1st Baron Seymour of Sudeley
This high-ranking Nazi SS officer served as Hitler's liaison to Heinrich Himmler and became the Führer's brother-in-law-by-marriage through his wedding to Eva Braun's sister. Who is he?
Hermann Fegelein: German Nazi Waffen-SS commander (1906–1945)
Born Su Zhu, he succeeded Mao Zedong as China's top leader in the 1970s before being gradually eased out of power between 1978 and 1981 — who is he?
Hua Guofeng: Leader of China from 1976 to 1978.

In 1980 she co-founded what would become the world's largest animal rights organization, and a year later her partner's monkey photos triggered the first U.S. police raid on a research lab — who is she?
Ingrid Newkirk: British and American animal rights activist (born 1949)

Launched at Glenfinnan by Charles Edward Stuart, this attempt to reclaim the British throne for the exiled House of Stuart saw rebels take Edinburgh before retreating from Derby that December — which rebellion?

Jacobite rising of 1745: Attempt by the House of Stuart to regain the British throne. The last in a series of Jacobite risings that began in March 1689, it proved to be the end of Jacobitism as a major factor in British politics.
Before leading a breakaway nation from 1861 to 1865, this Mississippian served as U.S. secretary of war under President Franklin Pierce — who held the post no one else ever has?
Jefferson Davis: President of the Confederate States from 1861 to 1865.
Born in the Panama Canal Zone and a Navy aviator who survived the 1967 USS Forrestal fire, this Arizona senator became the Republican presidential nominee in 2008 — who is he?
John McCain: American politician and naval officer (1936–2018)

Though Romulus Augustulus is traditionally called the last Western Roman emperor, modern historians give that distinction to a man who fled to Dalmatia and kept claiming the title until his murder in 480. Who was he?
Julius Nepos: Western Roman emperor from 474 to 480.

Fluent in Mandarin from his honours studies in Chinese, this Labor leader served twice as Australia's prime minister — once 2007 to 2010, and again briefly in 2013 — before later becoming ambassador to the United States. Who is he?

Kevin Rudd: Prime Minister of Australia (2007–2010; 2013). Born in Nambour, Queensland, Rudd graduated from the Australian National University with honours in Chinese studies, and is fluent in Mandarin.

Founded by former Confederate soldiers during Reconstruction to oppose civil rights for the newly freed, this secret society is considered one of the earliest terrorist organizations in US history. Which group is this?
Ku Klux Klan: American white supremacist hate group.
According to the Book of Genesis, which third son of Jacob and Leah became the ancestor of a priestly Israelite tribe, and great-grandfather of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam?
Levi: Biblical figure and son of Jacob and Leah.
Nicknamed 'Toto,' this Argentine economist serves as Javier Milei's Minister of Economy after previously leading the Central Bank of Argentina in 2018 — who is he?

Founded in 1932 on land seized in Japan's invasion of Manchuria, this Axis-recognized "puppet state" was dressed up first as a republic and then a monarchy before dissolving in 1945 — what was it called?
Manchukuo: 1932–1945 Japanese puppet state in northern China.
The eighth U.S. president is the only one to have spoken English as a second language, having grown up in a Dutch-speaking New York community — who is he?
Martin Van Buren: President of the United States from 1837 to 1841.
The third wife of Emperor Claudius, this Roman noblewoman was allegedly executed after conspiring against her husband, her scandalous reputation later immortalized in art and literature — who is she?
Messalina: Roman empress from AD 41 to 48.
Killed during Hernán Cortés's seizure of Tenochtitlan, this ninth Aztec emperor presided over the empire at its largest territorial extent — who was he?
Moctezuma II: Tlahtoāni of the Aztec Empire until 1520.
Son of Mehmed III and Halime Sultan, this Ottoman ruler held the throne twice, briefly in 1617–1618 and again in 1622–1623 — who was he?
Mustafa I: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire (r. 1617–1618, 1622–1623)
On the eve of WWII, this British stockbroker quietly arranged the rescue of 669 mostly-Jewish children from Czechoslovakia, finding them homes and sponsors in Britain — who was he?
Nicholas Winton: British banker and humanitarian (1909–2015)
This retired Marine lieutenant colonel and Vietnam veteran devised the plan to divert Iran arms-sale profits to Contra rebels, testifying before Congress under limited immunity — who is he?

In 1925, this British physicist became the first to prove that radioactivity could transmute one chemical element into another, later winning a Nobel Prize and pioneering operational research for the Allied war effort — who is he?
Serving as Vietnam's eighth prime minister from 2021 to 2026, this former lieutenant general once led the Communist Party's organizing commission — who is he?

Phạm Minh Chính: Prime Minister of Vietnam from 2021 to 2026. Phạm Minh Chính (Vietnamese: [faːm˧˨ʔ mïŋ˧˧ t͡ɕïŋ˧˦]; born 10 December 1958) is a Vietnamese politician and former public security lieutenant general.
Nicknamed the 'Black Baron,' this scion of a Baltic German noble family became the last commander-in-chief of the White forces in southern Russia during the Civil War — who was he?

Modeled on a notorious wave of Revolutionary France violence, this campaign of political repression and mass executions was carried out by the Bolshevik secret police during the Russian Civil War — what is it called?
Red Terror: Bolshevik campaign of political repression and executions (1918–1922)
The first Philippine president from Mindanao and the oldest to take office at 71, this former Davao City mayor led the country from 2016 — who is it?
Rodrigo Duterte: President of the Philippines from 2016 to 2022.
Born Rozbih Khwushbudhan and trained as a Zoroastrian magus, this companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad converted to Islam after meeting him in Medina — who was he?

Salman the Persian: Companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. Muhammad specifically said "Salman is part of my Ahl al-Bayt." In meetings with the other companions, he was often referred to by the kunya Abu ʿAbdullah.

Touched off by the staged 1931 Mukden incident and the puppet state of Manchukuo, this 1937–1945 conflict — China's largest war of the 20th century — is often called the start of World War II in Asia. What was it?
Second Sino-Japanese War: 1937–1945 conflict in East Asia. It is often regarded as the beginning of World War II in Asia, as the wars became heavily intertwined after Japan's entry into World War II.

Known as 'The Destroyer' within the Hindu trinity alongside Brahma and Vishnu, this deity is the Supreme Lord who creates, protects, and transforms the universe in one major tradition. Who is this god?
Shiva: Major deity in Hinduism. Shiva is one of the five equivalent deities in Panchayatana puja of the Smarta tradition of Hinduism.
A Thracian gladiator born near the Strymon river, this figure led an escaped-slave uprising against the Roman Republic known as the Third Servile War — who was he?
Spartacus: Thracian gladiator who led a slave revolt. Spartacus is described to be born near the Strymon river, in Thrace (now known as Bulgaria), possibly from the Maedi tribe.
Sparked by Arab Spring protests against Bashar al-Assad in March 2011, this nearly 14-year conflict ended with the regime's fall in December 2024 — what is it?
Syrian civil war: 2011–2024 armed conflict in Syria.

Ruling the Ostrogothic Kingdom of Italy from 493 to 526 and later regent of the Visigoths too, this king received the old Western imperial regalia from Constantinople and was addressed by Italy's aristocracy as princeps. Who was he?
Theodoric the Great: King of Italy from 493 to 526. As ruler of the combined Gothic realms, Theodoric controlled an empire stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Adriatic Sea.

Breaking out in 1990 between Moldovan government forces and pro-separatist fighters backed by Russia's 14th Army, this conflict over a breakaway region ended with a ceasefire in July 1992 that still holds — which conflict?
Transnistrian War: 1990–1992 separatist conflict in Moldova. Cojocaru, the Moldovan defeat in this war directly led to implementation of Moldovan neutrality.
This Roman goddess of love and beauty was claimed as an ancestor by Julius Caesar through her son Aeneas, survivor of the fall of Troy?
Venus (mythology): Ancient Roman goddess of love, sex and fertility.
This Kenyan activist founded the tree-planting Green Belt Movement and in 2004 became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Who was she?
After an evangelical conversion in 1785, this Yorkshire MP spent two decades leading the parliamentary fight that ended Britain's slave trade — who was he?
William Wilberforce: English politician and abolitionist (1759–1833)
Once called 'perhaps the most famous singer alive' in much of Africa, this Senegalese star helped develop the mbalax genre and even served as his country's Minister of Tourism — who is he?
Youssou N'Dour: Senegalese politician and musician (born 1959)
Who among these four was born earliest?
Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four. After helping found Shu Han, Zhuge Liang exercised near-total authority over both civil and military affairs.
Who among these was born first?
Emanuel Swedenborg (born 1688) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Which of these is a physicist?
John Logie Baird is a physicist. In 1928, the Baird Television Development Company achieved the first transatlantic television transmission.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
What is the atomic number of Nihonium?
Nihonium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Nh and atomic number 113.
What is the atomic number of Strontium?
Strontium is a chemical element; it has symbol Sr and atomic number 38.
In what year did Edward Teller die?
Edward Teller: Born in Austria-Hungary in 1908, Teller emigrated to the US in the 1930s, one of the many so-called "Martians", a group of Hungarian scientist émigrés.
In what year was Oxygen discovered?
Oxygen is a chemical element; it has the symbol O and its atomic number is 8.
Potassium chloride: Pfizer. Potassium chloride (KCl, or potassium salt) is a metal halide salt composed of potassium and chlorine.
In which country is Embraer E-Jet E2 family based?
Embraer E-Jet E2 family: Brazil. The Embraer E-Jet E2 family is a series of four-abreast narrow-body regional jet airliners designed and produced by the Brazilian aircraft manufacturer Embraer.
Who is credited with discovering Molybdenum?
Molybdenum: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.
Who is credited with discovering Serotonin?
Serotonin: Arda Green. It is involved in mood, cognition, reward, learning, memory, and physiological processes such as vomiting and vasoconstriction.
Who is credited with discovering Beryllium?
Beryllium: Louis Nicolas Vauquelin. Beryllium is a chemical element; it has symbol Be and atomic number 4.
Stretching from the thoracic diaphragm to the pelvic brim, this body region sits between the chest and the pelvis — which body part?
Abdomen (also belly or stomach in vertebrates, or metasoma in arthropods) is the front part of the torso between the thorax (chest) and pelvis in humans and in other vertebrates.
This English academic and broadcaster, an anatomist and archaeologist by training, was president of the charity Humanists UK from 2019 to 2022 — who is she?
Alice Roberts (born 19 May 1973) is an English academic, anatomist, archaeologist, TV presenter and author.
This symptom, not a diagnosis by itself, refers to a loss of appetite in humans and — under the name 'inappetence' — in animals from dogs to goats. Which symptom?
Anorexia (symptom) is a medical term for a loss of appetite.
Doctors reach for this NSAID not just for aches but to treat Kawasaki disease and rheumatic fever — and it's famous for its blood-thinning effect on platelets. What is it?
Aspirin is the genericized trademark for acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to reduce pain, fever, and inflammation, and as an antithrombotic.
Designed to replace the aging Tu-126 'Moss,' this Soviet early-warning aircraft saw only about 42 built before the USSR's breakup ended production in 1992 — what is it?
Beriev A-50 (NATO reporting name: Mainstay) is a Soviet-origin airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft that is based on the Ilyushin Il-76 transport plane.
Caused by a toxin that thrives in low-oxygen conditions — the same one sold cosmetically as 'botox' — this rare illness brings blurred vision and creeping paralysis but rarely a fever. What is it?
Botulism is a rare and potentially fatal illness caused by botulinum toxin (commonly referred to as botox), which is produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum.

First synthesized in 1950 by bombarding curium with helium-4 ions, this synthetic actinide element carries atomic number 98, symbol Cf, and the second-highest atomic mass of any element — which element?
Californium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cf and atomic number 98.
Discovered in 1801 by Giuseppe Piazzi and initially hailed as a new planet, this object in the main asteroid belt is now the only recognized dwarf planet orbiting within Neptune's path — what is it?
Ceres (dwarf planet) is a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
Marked by a stopped heartbeat and halted breathing, this reversible-sounding medical state was given its name once CPR and defibrillation made post-arrest resuscitation possible — what's it called?
Clinical death is the medical term for cessation of blood circulation and breathing, the two criteria necessary to sustain the lives of human beings and of many other organisms.
What's the statistical term for the extent to which two variables are linearly related — famously not the same thing as causation?
Correlation is a type of statistical relationship between two random variables or bivariate data.
Specialists in this branch of medicine handle skin infections, cancers, hair loss, and cosmetic concerns, sometimes even life-threatening conditions like severe burns — which medical field?
Dermatology is the branch of medicine dealing with the skin.
Partly blinded in a childhood fishing accident, this Alabama-born naturalist turned to insects, co-developed the theory of island biogeography, and founded the field of sociobiology. Who is he?
E. O. Wilson (June 10, 1929 - December 26, 2021) was an American biologist, naturalist, ecologist, and entomologist who developed the field of sociobiology.
Comprising around 50 species mostly found in the tropics, this fungal genus infects rye, wheat, barley, and other grasses, producing toxic alkaloids — name the group of fungi?
Ergot is a group of fungi of the genus Claviceps. The most prominent member of this group is Claviceps purpurea (rye ergot fungus).
This plant genus of roughly 850 species includes woody trees, vines, and epiphytes native to the tropics, though only two species are widely cultivated for their sweet fruit — what genus is it?
Ficus (or) is a genus of about 850 species of woody trees, shrubs, vines, epiphytes and hemiepiphytes in the family Moraceae.
This scholarly discipline covers the link between food and culture, from recipes and regional cooking styles to the rigorous science of good eating — what's it called?

Gastronomy is the study of the relationship between food and culture, the art of preparing and serving rich or delicate and appetizing food, the cooking styles of particular regions, and the science of good eating.
Flown by both the U.S. Navy and Britain's Royal Navy under the name Martlet, this 1940 carrier fighter went toe-to-toe with the Mitsubishi Zero over the Pacific — which aircraft?
Grumman F4F Wildcat is an American carrier-based fighter aircraft that entered service in 1940 with the United States Navy and the British Royal Navy.

Named from the Greek for 'different wings' because most species have forewings that are part membrane, part hardened shell, this group of 40,000 insect species is the one most consistently called 'true bugs' — name this insect group?
Heteroptera are a group of about 40,000 species of insects in the order Hemiptera.
Marked by shivering and confusion in mild cases and hallucinations or paradoxical undressing in severe cases, this condition is defined as a body core temperature below 35°C (95°F) — name it?
Hypothermia is defined as a body core temperature below 35.0 C (95.0 F) in humans.

Once found as far north as Texas's Lower Rio Grande Valley but now extirpated from the US, this slender wild cat comes in gray and red color morphs, ranging from Mexico to Argentina — what animal is it?
Jaguarundi (Herpailurus yagouaroundi); or is a wild cat native to the Americas.
Endemic to New Caledonia's mountain forests, this bluish-grey, nearly flightless bird sports bright red legs and unique nasal corns shared by no other bird — what is it?
Kagu (Rhynochetos jubatus) is a crested, long-legged, and bluish-grey bird endemic to the dense mountain forests of New Caledonia.
Caused by a specific type of waterborne bacteria, this form of atypical pneumonia brings cough, fever, muscle pain, and headache within days of exposure — what's it called?
Legionnaires' disease is a form of atypical pneumonia caused by any species of Legionella bacteria, quite often Legionella pneumophila.
Named for antennae often longer than its own body, this insect family boasts over 35,000 species and gets its name from a Greek myth about a shepherd transformed after angering nymphs — which group?
Longhorn beetle (Cerambycidae), also known as long-horned or longicorns (whose larvae are often referred to as roundheaded borers), are a large family of beetles, with over 35,000 species described.
This computer scientist led the on-board flight software for NASA's Apollo Guidance Computer and is credited with coining the very term 'software engineering' — who is she?
Margaret Hamilton (software engineer) (ne Heafield; born August 17, 1936) is an American computer scientist.
This hedge fund manager and licensed physician was among the first to predict and profit from the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis, later portrayed on screen in The Big Short. Who is he?
Michael Burry (born June 19, 1971) is an American investor, hedge fund manager, and licensed physician.
One of the four basic animal tissue types, this contractile tissue comes in skeletal, cardiac, and smooth forms and relies on the proteins actin and myosin to generate movement — name the tissue?
Muscle is a specialised soft tissue, one of the four basic types of animal tissues.
Once confused with its chemical twin tantalum, this element with atomic number 41 resists corrosion so well it's used in earrings for people allergic to nickel — which element?
Niobium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nb (formerly columbium, Cb) and atomic number 41.
Known for causing bones that fracture easily, this group of genetic disorders can also produce blue-tinted eye whites, short stature, and hearing loss. Name the condition?
Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), colloquially known as brittle bone disease, is a group of genetic disorders that all result in bones that break easily.
Favored by royalty in the Chinese Imperial court, this toy dog breed originated in China's ancient capital — name the breed?
Pekingese (also spelled Pekinese) is a breed of toy dog, originating in China.

A perennial legume native to the Eastern Hemisphere, this crop is a staple across the Indian Subcontinent, Africa and the Caribbean despite a name that sounds more like a bird than a bean. What is it?
Pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan) is a perennial legume from the family Fabaceae native to the Eastern Hemisphere.

Native to North American grasslands, these burrowing, herbivorous ground squirrels come in five species, black-tailed, white-tailed, Gunnison's, Utah, and Mexican. Name this genus, Cynomys, by its common two-word name?
Prairie dog (genus Cynomys) are herbivorous burrowing ground squirrels native to the grasslands of North America.

This small herbivore belongs to the family Leporidae alongside hares, and the European species of its genus has been introduced to every continent except Antarctica — what bouncy little prey animal is it?
Rabbit are small mammals in the family Leporidae (which also includes the hares), which is in the order Lagomorpha (which also includes pikas).

Nicknamed 'Il Professore' for his academic background, this Italian politician served as European Commission President from 1999 to 2004 and was twice his country's prime minister, first after leading The Olive Tree coalition to victory — who is he?

Romano Prodi (born 9 August 1939) is an Italian politician who served as President of the European Commission from 1999 to 2004 and twice as Prime Minister of Italy, from 1996 to 1998, and again from 2006 to 2008.

These colorful predatory marine animals — single polyps usually anchored by their base — are named after a terrestrial flower and, unlike their jellyfish relatives, skip the medusa stage entirely; what are they?
Sea anemone (-) are a group of predatory marine invertebrate animals constituting the order Actiniaria.
Despite the name, this digestive organ is about 6.5 metres long; it's just narrower in diameter than its large counterpart. What organ is it?
Small intestine is an organ in the gastrointestinal tract where most of the absorption of nutrients from food takes place.
Known by his online username 'spez,' this web developer co-founded an airfare search engine before leading the world's seventh most-visited website as CEO — who is he?
Steve Huffman (born 1983 or 1984), also known by his Reddit username spez, is an American web developer and entrepreneur.
Born in 1946, this American serial killer often posed as an authority figure or feigned injury to lure young women to his car before assaulting and murdering them — who was he?
Ted Bundy (n Cowell; November 24, 1946 - January 24, 1989) was an American serial killer who kidnapped, raped and murdered dozens of young women and girls throughout 1974, 1975, and 1978.
A nasty complication of this inflamed-throat illness goes by the wonderfully old-fashioned name 'quinsy,' or peritonsillar abscess — what's the underlying condition?
Tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils in the upper part of the throat.
This phenolic aldehyde is the primary component of the vanilla bean's extract — and its synthetic version now flavors more foods than the natural one does. What is it?
Vanillin is an organic compound with the molecular formula C8H8O3.
Neither an insect nor a parasite despite its common name, this terrestrial crustacean is one of the few of its kind to have colonized dry land, likely since the late Paleozoic — what is it?
Woodlouse are terrestrial isopods in the suborder Oniscidea.
Formed when acetic acid combines with a base, this ion is also nature's most common building block for biosynthesis — what is it?
Acetate: Salt formed from acetic acid and a base.
Also known as thymol seeds, bishop's weed, or carom, this Apiaceae herb's fruit is often mistaken for lovage seed — what is it?
Sometimes called 'pigweed,' this genus of plants is grown worldwide as a leaf vegetable and for its edible grain — which genus?
Amaranth: Genus of plants. The plant can grow from 1 to 2.5 metres (3 to 8 feet) tall with a succulent, hollow stem.
Comprising the talocrural, subtalar, and inferior tibiofibular joints, this region where the foot meets the leg enables dorsiflexion and plantarflexion — which body part?
Ankle: Region where the foot and the leg meet. The ankle includes three joints: the ankle joint proper or talocrural joint, the subtalar joint, and the inferior tibiofibular joint.
The fourth-brightest star in the night sky and the brightest in the northern hemisphere, this aging red giant in Boötes has ballooned to 25 times the Sun's size despite sharing its mass — what is it?
Arcturus: Brightest star in the constellation Boötes. It has the Bayer designation α Boötis, which is Latinized to Alpha Boötis and abbreviated Alpha Boo or α Boo.

Despite its name being something of a misnomer, this herding dog breed was developed in California and takes its name from imported collies that arrived alongside sheep from Down Under — what breed is it?
Australian Shepherd: American breed of dog. The Australian Shepherd, also known as the Aussie, is a breed of herding dog from the United States.
This inflammatory condition causes recurring, painful mouth sores along with eye inflammation and arthritis, and is diagnosed after at least three sore outbreaks in a year — which condition?
Behçet's disease: Inflammatory disorder. Behçet's disease or Behçet's syndrome (BD; sometimes written Behcet) is a type of inflammatory disorder which affects multiple parts of the body.
Rich in vitamin C and polyphenols, this deciduous shrub's glossy dark berries are cooked into jams and syrups or fermented into cassis — what is it?
Blackcurrant: Species of flowering plant in the gooseberry family Grossulariaceae.
Named from Greek words for 'slow' and 'heart,' this condition means a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute — sometimes normal in well-conditioned athletes — which condition?
Bradycardia: Heart rate below the normal range.
Common in cancer, heart failure, and other serious illnesses, this syndrome causes muscle wasting that better nutrition alone can't reverse — what is it?
In 1886 this German engineer patented what's considered the first practical automobile, and his Mannheim company later merged with Daimler — who is he?
Carl Benz: German designer and engineer (1844–1929)
Documented anatomically since the time of Hippocrates over 2,000 years ago, this roughly 4-centimeter-long fibromuscular organ connects the vagina to the uterine cavity. What structure is this?
Cervix: Lower part of the uterus in the female reproductive system.
This Dutch scientist discovered Saturn's largest moon and invented the pendulum clock, the most accurate timekeeper for nearly three centuries — who is he?
Christiaan Huygens: Dutch mathematician and physicist (1629–1695)
Thought extinct since the age of dinosaurs 66 million years ago, this lobe-finned fish was found alive off the west Indian Ocean, more closely related to lungfish than typical fish — what is it?
A heart disease involving reduced blood flow to cardiac muscle due to buildup of plaque in heart arteries — the most common cardiovascular disease. What is it?
Coronary artery disease: Reduction of blood flow to the heart. Procedures such as percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or coronary artery bypass surgery (CABG) may be used in severe disease.
Named after the bladder because it was first found in urine, this amino acid carries a thiol group that lets it forge the disulfide bonds holding many proteins together. Which amino acid is it?
Cysteine: Proteinogenic amino acid. Cysteine (symbol Cys or C) is a semiessential proteinogenic amino acid with the formula HS−CH2−CH(NH2)−COOH.

Doctors once spotted this endocrine condition by its three Ps — polydipsia, polyuria, and polyphagia, or excessive thirst, urination, and hunger — all tracing back to trouble with insulin. Which disease is it?
Diabetes: Group of endocrine diseases characterized by high blood sugar levels.
Working alongside biochemist Katalin Karikó on nucleoside base modifications, this University of Pennsylvania immunologist shared the 2023 Nobel Prize for enabling COVID-19 mRNA vaccines — who is he?
Drew Weissman: American physician and immunologist (born 1959)
First described in 1821, this family of large herbivorous mammals features a snout modified into a trunk and includes extinct relatives such as mammoths — which taxonomic family?
Elephantidae: Family of mammals. The family was first described by John Edward Gray in 1821, and later assigned to taxonomic ranks within the order Proboscidea.

Arising in the food pipe that runs between the throat and the stomach, this disease's two main subtypes are a squamous-cell form common in the developing world and a glandular form more common in developed nations. What is it?
Esophageal cancer: Malignant neoplastic disease of the esophagus.
Carried out by the lungs, kidneys, and skin in vertebrates, this bodily process rids the body of metabolic byproducts like urea, carbon dioxide, and uric acid — what is it called?
Excretion: Elimination of metabolic waste products by an organism.

Sometimes nicknamed a 'cat' though it's actually the sole living member of its own genus in the weasel family, this North American forest mammal has been trapped for its fur since the 1700s — what is it?
Fisher (animal): Species of small, carnivorous mammal native to North America.

Unlike plants, this kingdom of life can't photosynthesize, and unlike most things, it has chitin in its cell walls — feeding instead by oozing digestive enzymes out and absorbing what dissolves. What group includes yeasts, molds, and mushrooms?
Fungus: Organism belonging to kingdom Fungi.
Endemic to China and sporting a handy 'thumb' on its forepaw to grip bamboo, this black-and-white bear weighs in around 100 to 115 kg — what animal is it?
Giant panda: Species of bear. The giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca), also known as the panda bear or simply panda, is a bear species endemic to China.
This large, widely distributed white wading bird nests in colonies built in trees near water and is now expanding its range into northern Europe — which species?
Great egret: Species of bird. The great egret (Ardea alba), also known as the common egret, large egret, great white egret, or great white heron, is a large, widely distributed egret.

Recognizable by V-shaped nostrils and a layer of blubber that keeps it warm in Arctic and temperate coastal waters, this pinniped is the most widely distributed of its kind and can weigh up to 370 pounds — which species?
Harbor seal: Species of pinniped. Blubber under the seal's skin helps to maintain body temperature.

Bred by Polynesians in the pre-Columbian era from two Pacific island species, this tropical flowering plant is the national flower of Malaysia and the unofficial national flower of Haiti — what is it?
Hibiscus × rosa-sinensis: Hybrid species of flowering plant. It is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant in the tropics and subtropics.
Carl Wilhelm Scheele pinned down this gas's composition in 1777; it's flammable, smells of rotten eggs, and kills by blocking cellular respiration much like cyanide — what colorless compound is it?
Hydrogen sulfide: Poisonous and flammable gas. Hydrogen sulfide (preferred IUPAC name and American English) or hydrogen sulphide (Commonwealth English) is a chemical compound with the formula H2S.
Patented in 1961 and used to fight fever, pain and inflammation by blocking the cyclooxygenase enzyme, this drug sits on the WHO's List of Essential Medicines — what is it?

His 1962 book The Calculus of Consent launched a theory of how politicians' and bureaucrats' self-interest shapes their decisions, earning him the 1986 Nobel in economics — which founder of public choice theory is this?
James M. Buchanan: American economist and Nobel Laureate (1919–2013)
Dubbed the 'Angel of Death,' this German physician held doctorates in both anthropology and medicine before joining the SS and selecting Auschwitz prisoners for the gas chambers — who was he?
Josef Mengele: Nazi SS doctor at Auschwitz (1911–1979)
Also called German turnip despite not being related to true turnips, this stout cabbage cultivar can be eaten raw or cooked, stem and leaves alike — what vegetable?
Kohlrabi: Biennial cultivar of wild cabbage.
Also known as Peruvian ginseng, this Andean root crop is grown at high altitude in Peru and Bolivia and exported worldwide as a dietary powder — what plant is it?
Lepidium meyenii: Plant species native to South America.
Developed under Kelly Johnson's Skunk Works team after the discovery of Germany's Me 262, this aircraft became the first jet fighter flown operationally by U.S. forces in World War II — which jet?
Lockheed P-80 Shooting Star: First jet aircraft in U.S. operational service.
Known historically as 'magnesia alba' to distinguish it from a manganese-containing mineral called 'magnesia nigra,' this white hygroscopic solid has the formula MgO — what is it?
Magnesium oxide: Chemical compound naturally occurring as periclase.
Widely brewed as a calming herbal tea despite limited clinical evidence for its effects, this annual plant in the daisy family goes by the nickname 'scented mayweed' — which plant?
Matricaria chamomilla: Species of flowering plant.
First isolated in 1921 and encoded by the codon AUG, this essential amino acid also serves as the precursor to cysteine — which amino acid is this?
Following the S phase and ending in cytokinesis, this equational cell division splits replicated chromosomes into two genetically identical daughter nuclei — what is the process called?
Mitosis: Cell division into two identical cells. Mitosis is a part of the cell cycle in eukaryotic cells in which replicated chromosomes are separated into two new nuclei.
Despite its name, this blister-agent chemical weapon isn't always gaseous, and to this day there is no antidote for exposure to it — what is it?
Mustard gas: Chemical warfare agent. There is no preventive agent against mustard gas, with protection depending entirely on skin and airways protection, and no antidote exists for mustard poisoning.
This medical specialty diagnoses and treats disorders of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves, from epilepsy and stroke to Parkinson's disease — which field?
Neurology: Medical specialty dealing with disorders of the nervous system.
Named for a discredited belief that it 'rows' itself with its pelvic fins, this family of long pelagic fish includes the longest bony fish alive at up to 8 meters?
Oarfish: Pelagic lampriform fish belonging to Regalecidae.
Derived from an ancient Roman unit called the uncia, this measure comes in an avoirdupois version equal to 1/16 of a pound and a heavier troy version used for precious metals — what unit is it?
Ounce: Unit of mass. The ounce is any of several different units of mass, weight, or volume and is derived almost unchanged from the uncia, an Ancient Roman unit of measurement.
He earned a PhD in physics from Cambridge for the first-ever thesis on quantum mechanics, then shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Erwin Schrödinger — who is he?
Turning colorless in acid and a fuchsia pink in base, this phthalein dye is a favorite indicator for acid-base titrations — what is it?
Phenolphthalein: pH indicator that turns pink in basic solution.
Its name comes from the Spanish for 'little silver,' yet this dense, stubbornly unreactive metal — element 78 — is so scarce only a few hundred tonnes are mined a year. Which one?
Platinum: Chemical element with atomic number 78 (Pt)

A trained engineer by profession, this royal consort married King Mohammed VI in 2002, becoming the first publicly acknowledged wife of a reigning monarch there to hold an official title, before their discreet 2018 divorce. Who is she?
Princess Lalla Salma of Morocco: Moroccan royal (born 1978)
Imagine a benzene ring with one CH swapped for a nitrogen atom: the result is this flammable, fish-smelling liquid once distilled from coal tar and now made at 20,000 tons a year — what is it?
Known in North America as caribou, this circumpolar deer species ranges from the tiny Svalbard subspecies to the much larger Osborn's version roaming the Arctic tundra — which animal is it?
Reindeer: Species of deer. It is the only representative of the genus Rangifer.

This chronic skin condition causes facial redness, small dilated blood vessels, and in severe cases an enlarged red nose, and can be triggered by spicy food, alcohol, or sun exposure — which condition?
Rosacea: Skin condition, usually on the face.
Nicknamed 'mother-in-law's tongue' and 'snake plant,' this genus of stiff, sword-leaved succulents from Africa and southern Asia is now classified within Dracaena — which genus?
About 90% of this mood-regulating neurotransmitter is actually made in your gut, where it controls intestinal movement, rather than the brain — also known as 5-HT, what is it?
Serotonin: Monoamine neurotransmitter. It is involved in mood, cognition, reward, learning, memory, and physiological processes such as vomiting and vasoconstriction.
With the formula CH3COONa, this colorless, moisture-absorbing compound is the salt formed from acetic acid — what is it called?
Named in 1880 from Greek words meaning 'bunch of grapes,' this genus of spherical, grape-clustered bacteria can grow with or without oxygen — which genus?
Among the largest flighted birds in their range, these waterfowl of genus Cygnus typically mate for life and lay three to eight eggs per clutch — what are they?
Swan: Tribe of large water birds.
Made of collagen like its bone-to-bone cousin the ligament, this tough band of connective tissue instead links muscle to bone, and there are about 4,000 of them in your body — what is it called?
Tendon: Type of tissue that connects muscle to bone.
Native to Africa and the Middle East, this freshwater fish has become a global aquaculture staple but can turn invasive in warm habitats like Australia — which fish?
Tilapia: Common name for many species of fish.
This essential amino acid, which the body can't make on its own, is a precursor to serotonin, melatonin, and vitamin B3 — which amino acid?

Discovered in 1801 by a Spanish-Mexican scientist but only confirmed as a new element in 1830, this hard silvery-grey transition metal takes its name from a Scandinavian goddess of beauty — what element is it?
Vanadium: Chemical element with atomic number 23 (V)
Equal to seven days, this standard calendrical period sits between a single day and a month — despite ancient Egyptians preferring a ten-day version, what unit of time is it?
Week: Time unit equal to seven days. The days of the week are often used to set work days, rest days, and holy days.

Named after a 19th-century British scientist but actually first developed by Leonhard Euler in 1727, this mechanical property measures a solid material's stiffness under tension or compression — what is it called?

Young's modulus: Mechanical property that measures stiffness of a solid material. As such, Young's modulus is similar and proportional to the spring constant in Hooke's law, but with dimensions of pressure instead of force per distance.
The symbol for oganesson is Og. Oganesson is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Og and atomic number 118.
Thulium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for thulium is Tm. Thulium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tm and atomic number 69.

Who among these is a comedian?
Arsenio Hall is a comedian. Arsenio Hall (born February 12, 1956) is an American comedian, actor and talk show host.
In what year was Truman Capote born?
Truman Capote: Capote had a troubled childhood caused by his parents' divorce, a long absence from his mother, and multiple moves.
In what year was Alec Baldwin born?
Alec Baldwin: Alexander Rae Baldwin III (born April 3, 1958) is an American actor and film producer.

Annette Bening: Annette Carol Bening (born May 29, 1958) is an American actress.
In what year was Tom Selleck born?
Tom Selleck: Thomas William Selleck (born January 29, 1945) is an American actor.
In what year was Akshay Kumar born?
Akshay Kumar: Kumar is one of the most prolific actors in Indian cinema.
In what year was Judi Dench born?
Judi Dench: Dame Judith Olivia Dench (born 9 December 1934) is an English actress.
In what year was Jeffrey Dean Morgan born?
Jeffrey Dean Morgan (born April 22, 1966) is an American actor.
In what year was Josh Brolin born?
Josh Brolin: Josh James Brolin (born February 12, 1968) is an American actor and producer.

James Marsden: James Paul Marsden (born September 18, 1973) is an American actor.
In what year was Olivia Colman born?
Olivia Colman: A graduate of the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, Colman's breakthrough came in the Channel 4 sitcom Peep Show (2003–2015).
